solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Very square Aussie is upset if I am drunk (4,6)

indicatorNotes.upset: the letters of the phrase are knocked over and rearranged

annotation.surface: An Australian admits to being thoroughly straight-laced, unless he has had a few.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like the anagram indicator, but it is part of the fodder; 'upset' does the stirring. Square here means honest, as in a square deal.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair dinkum is Australian slang for genuine or honest, so a thoroughly square dealing Aussie is fair dinkum.

entries.clue: Newspaper introducing fantastic feature (5)

indicatorNotes.introducing: the newspaper takes the next word into itself

annotation.surface: A paper runs a splendid special article.
annotation.walkthrough: The FT (Financial Times) is the stock crossword newspaper. 'Feature' in a newspaper surface suggests an article, but here it means an aspect.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a facet, literally one face of a cut gem, is by extension one aspect or feature of anything.

entries.clue: Where you see marathon athletes at the end of the day? (2,3,4,3)

annotation.definition2: at the end of the day

blocks.note: read literally: the place a marathon runner is found is out on a lengthy race

blocks.clueFragment: at the end of the day

annotation.surface: A question about spotting marathon runners as the evening closes in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At the end of the day' reads as a time of evening, but it is the idiom meaning 'ultimately', which is what 'in the long run' also means.
annotation.definitionFit: Both 'in the long run' and 'at the end of the day' mean eventually, when all is said and done.

entries.clue: Author ate up approval, finally (4)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, writing a word upwards reverses it

annotation.surface: A writer greedily consumes praise, at last.
annotation.walkthrough: Roald Dahl wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. 'Ate up' sounds like one phrase for eating everything, but 'up' is doing separate work on HAD.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Roald Dahl, who wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, is one author among many.

entries.clue: Elderly relative put up in French city (6)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, writing a word upwards reverses it

annotation.surface: Granny is being housed somewhere in France.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put up in' reads as 'accommodated in', but 'in' is only the link to the city; 'up' reverses SET.
annotation.definitionFit: Nantes is a city in western France on the Loire.

entries.clue: All that is in place for learning poetry (8)

annotation.surface: Everything that happens at school to help pupils learn poems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'All that is' looks like the start of an ordinary sentence, but it is the definition: everything that exists.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym at its widest: the cosmos, everything in existence, is exactly 'all that is'.

entries.clue: Awesome rants about former country (7,5)

indicatorNotes.about: the letters are turned about into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone delivers magnificent tirades concerning a nation that no longer exists.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning', but it is the anagram indicator. The country is 'former' because it dropped 'Western' from its name in 1997.
annotation.definitionFit: Western Samoa was the name of the Pacific nation now called simply Samoa.

entries.clue: Grand noblewoman welcomes Liberal with a smile? (6)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: the noblewoman takes the Liberal inside her

annotation.surface: A stately aristocrat greets a political visitor, all smiles.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'with a smile' is a loose definition: doing something gladly, you might well smile.
annotation.definitionFit: To do something gladly is to do it willingly and happily, as if with a smile.

entries.clue: Get it and become popular (5,2)

blocks.note: get it = understand, grasp the point

annotation.surface: Advice to understand something and gain fans.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses of the phrasal verb: to grasp an idea, and for a trend to spread.
annotation.definitionFit: To catch on is both to understand (get it) and to become widely popular.

entries.clue: Best possible current agreement (5)

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current

annotation.surface: The most favourable arrangement on offer right now.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'present', but it is electric current, written I in physics.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the adjective describes a perfect example of its kind, the best possible.

entries.clue: Pretty short sound made by a bird (4)

indicatorNotes.short: something short falls short of its full length, so the word stops a letter early

blocks.note: a tweet is a bird's chirp; lose its last T

annotation.surface: A rather brief chirp from a bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pretty short' reads as 'fairly short', but 'Pretty' is the definition and 'short' the instruction. Twee is a mainly British word for sugary, overly quaint prettiness.
annotation.definitionFit: Twee means excessively or affectedly pretty, sweet or quaint.

entries.clue: Disliked being emailed again by senior journalist (8)

annotation.surface: Someone was irritated that the editor forwarded their email a second time.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a grudge over a forwarded email; the trick is reading the definition's sense of resenting into a word that also means 'sent again'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: to take something with bitter displeasure is to dislike it.

entries.clue: In a way, we are essentially breaking into a part of the Web (2,2,4)

indicatorNotes.essentially: take the essence, the middle letter, of 'are'
indicatorNotes.breaking into: the letters burst inside the other word

annotation.surface: Some of us are, in a sense, hacking into an internet page.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In a way' opens the clue as if it were an aside, but it is the definition. 'Essentially' only touches 'are', taking its heart.
annotation.definitionFit: 'As it were' hedges a phrase, meaning so to speak, or in a way.

entries.clue: Regular appearances from wild, foolish megastars (5)

indicatorNotes.Regular appearances from: take letters at regular intervals, here every second one

annotation.surface: Crazy celebrities keep turning up.
annotation.walkthrough: The indicator reads like a remark about stars' public appearances; it means every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: idolised celebrities, worshipped by fans, are the megastars of the surface.

entries.clue: International group of performers still together (6)

blocks.note: an act, such as a band

annotation.surface: A global touring band still hasn't split up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a band that has not broken up; the definition is the plain sense of unbroken.
annotation.definitionFit: Intact means whole, undamaged, still together.

entries.clue: Bad-tempered and certainly devoid of energy (5)

indicatorNotes.devoid of: devoid of means completely lacking, so the word must go without the E

annotation.surface: Someone grumpy and utterly listless.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a description of a tired, grumpy person; 'energy' is just E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the adjective describes someone sullen and rude, which is to say bad-tempered.

entries.clue: Strand of polymer in one type of fabric (6)

indicatorNotes.Strand of: a thread pulled out of the following words

annotation.surface: A fibre of plastic found in a certain textile.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about fibres and fabric, so 'Strand' sounds like a thread rather than a hint to lift letters out.
annotation.definitionFit: Merino is a fine wool fabric from merino sheep.

entries.clue: Roget possibly includes the synonym for “well-organised” (8)

indicatorNotes.possibly: Roget in some other possible arrangement
indicatorNotes.includes: the rearranged letters take THE inside

annotation.surface: A thesaurus lookup: Roget's gives a word meaning organised.
annotation.walkthrough: Roget's Thesaurus is the classic book of synonyms, so the clue sounds like a reference lookup. 'Possibly' rearranges ROGET, and THE goes inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone together is well-organised and self-possessed.

entries.clue: It’s highly unlikely some stufF IS Actually returned (2,2)

indicatorNotes.some: only some of the letters are used
indicatorNotes.returned: something returned comes back the way it went, so the letters are read in the reverse direction

blocks.note: the letters sit across three words, stuF IS Actually, and read right to left

annotation.surface: A doubter says there's little chance any goods will really come back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As if!' is the scornful exclamation meaning that will never happen.
annotation.definitionFit: The exclamation 'As if!' means it's highly unlikely.

entries.clue: Might put pressure on (5)

blocks.note: might as a noun = strength, power

annotation.surface: Someone may lean on another person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Might' reads as the verb 'may', but it is the noun meaning power.
annotation.definitionFit: Force is both might (power) and to put pressure on someone.

entries.clue: A police department is far from basic? (4)

blocks.note: CID = Criminal Investigation Department, British detectives

annotation.surface: A remark that a police unit is sophisticated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Basic' in chemistry means alkaline, the opposite of acid; the question mark flags that pun on 'simple'.
annotation.definitionFit: An acid is chemically the opposite of a base, so it is far from basic.

entries.clue: Two people wanting large car (5)

annotation.surface: A pair of people want a big vehicle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' reads as desiring, but it means lacking, so the L for large leaves COUPLE.
annotation.definitionFit: A coupe is a two-door car with a fixed roof.

entries.clue: One entering revenue receipts on the left hand side (7)

indicatorNotes.on the left hand side: the leftmost letter of the word, its first

blocks.clueFragment: receipts on the left hand side

annotation.surface: A bookkeeper entering revenue receipts in the left-hand column of the ledger.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is accounts, where 'entering' means writing figures in; in the definition it means coming in. INCOMER is a British word for a newcomer to an area.
annotation.definitionFit: An incomer is someone who comes in, a newcomer.

entries.clue: Mediocre actors need to be changed (6-4)

indicatorNotes.to be changed: the letters must be altered into a new order

annotation.surface: Poor performers must be replaced.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a casting complaint; 'need' is fodder, not a link.
annotation.definitionFit: Second-rate means mediocre, of inferior quality.
